fetched_contents.text: Oxygen vacancies mediated enhanced photocatalytic activity of band gap engineered BaSn1−xCuxO3 towards methylene blue degradation under visible and sunlight Abstract Photocatalysis, an advanced oxidation process (AOP), has been well explored as a promising and sustainable technology for tackling environmental pollution. This method involves semiconductors which generate powerful reactive oxygen species, capable of breaking down organic pollutants, on excitation with appropriate light energy. Among the diverse range of oxide semiconductors explored, perovskite oxides are an important family. While BaSnO3 is a known perovskite photocatalyst, its intrinsic photocatalytic efficiency is limited by poor separation of charge carriers. To overcome this, a proven strategy is to create oxygen vacancies. These defects suppress electron–hole recombination leading to enhanced photocatalytic degradation. Hence, we have synthesized the system BaSn1−xCuxO3 (x = 0.0 to 0.2) and characterized well. Synthesis of the BaSn1−xCuxO3 series was successfully carried out via a facile solid-state reaction route. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirms the phase purity and cubic crystal structure. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) confirms the Ba–O, Sn–O, Cu–O vibrations. The surface morphology and particle size distribution examined using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) reveal that the particles are cubic in shape. The optical properties investigated using ultraviolet diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV-DRS) indicate the band gaps to be in the range of 3.15–2.42 eV. Photoluminescence study confirms the effective charge carrier separation on doping with Cu. Its photocatalytic activity under visible and sunlight using methylene blue (MB) as a model pollutant has been studied. Indeed, we could enhance the photocatalytic activity of BaSnO3 and Cu doping at the Sn site (x = 0.2) exhibits 8 times higher rate constant than the parent phase under visible light and 60 times higher under sunlight respectively. The degradation percentages of MB are more than 95% in the doped phase in 30 min in both visible & sunlight whereas the parent phase exhibits it in 3 h. The significantly enhanced activity can be attributed to the oxygen vacancies created due to the substitution of Sn4+ by Cu2+. We have also proposed a possible degradation pathway. This study constitutes the first documentation of the photocatalytic activity of BaSn1−xCuxO3, thereby opening new avenues for its potential applications in environmental remediation. ---------------------------------------- Copper doping in BaSnO3 creates oxygen vacancies and reduces the band gap, enhancing its photocatalytic activity under sunlight. 1. With the rapid development of industry and agriculture, serious water pollution results from the emission of many organic pollutants.1–4 Synthetic dyes, including methylene blue (MB), widely used in industries like textiles, pose significant health risks. These risks include carcinogenic effects, mutagenicity, dermatological issues, and other serious health problems.5–12 The most popular techniques for eliminating contaminants include chemical, biological, and physical adsorption techniques.13–15 In recent years, there has been a lot of interest in heterogeneous photocatalytic destruction of refractory organic contaminants from water by semiconductors.16,17 Perovskite-type semiconductor oxides have garnered significant interest for their photocatalytic properties, driven by their cost-effectiveness, exceptional catalytic performance, and environmental compatibility.18–20 The perovskite oxides of the general formula, ABO3, formed between the oxides of alkaline-earth metals (A = Ca, Sr, and Ba) and those of the group IV elements are of great industrial and technological importance. For photocatalytic pollutant degradation, a range of perovskite materials have been investigated, including, ASnO3 (A = Ca, Sr, Ba), LaCoO3, BaZrO3, and LaNiO3. Among these, BaSnO3, a simple cubic perovskite, is an electrical insulator characterized by a wide band gap of 3.1 eV.21,22 Properties of BaSnO3 have been modified by heterovalent substitutions both at Ba site (La3+) and Sn site (Nb5+, Ni2+, Cr3+, Mn3+, Sb5+, Fe3+) and studied for its magnetic, electrical properties.23–29 Fe3+ substitution30 only has been studied for its photocatalytic activity (for dye degradation) and it exhibits a degradation of 93% in 4 h which is much lower than the present study of Cu2+ substitution. fetched_contents.text: Oxygen vacancy enhanced photocatalytic activity of Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunction: iScience Highlights • The Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunction with oxygen vacancy is obtained by one-step method • The CO yield of Cu2O/TiO2 is 1.85 times that of TiO2, with 10.22 μmol g−1 h−1 • The performance is the best when the mass fraction of Cu is between 0.075%–0.55% • The free energy of Cu2O/TiO2Ov from ∗CO2 to ∗COOH is 0.088 eV lower than that of TiO2 Summary In this study, a method was developed to create oxygen vacancies in Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunctions. By varying the amounts of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), sodium citrate, and copper acetate, Cu2O/TiO2 with different Cu ratios were synthesized. Tests on CO2 photocatalytic reduction revealed that Cu2O/TiO2’s performance is influenced by Cu content. The ideal Cu mass fraction in Cu2O/TiO2, determined by inductively coupled plasma (ICP), is between 0.075% and 0.55%, with the highest CO yield being 10.22 μmol g−1 h−1, significantly surpassing pure TiO2. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy and electron paramagnetic resonance studies showed optimal oxygen vacancy in the most effective heterojunction. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicated a 0.088 eV lower energy barrier for ∗CO2 to ∗COOH conversion in Cu2O/TiO2 with oxygen vacancy compared to TiO2, suggesting that oxygen vacancies enhance photocatalytic activity. Graphical abstract Subject areas 1. Material chemistry 2. surface chemistry 3. physical chemistry Introduction TiO2 is one of the most widely studied semiconductors for environmental and energy issues.1,2,3- However, the photocatalytic efficiency of TiO2 is limited by its wide bandgap and high recombination rate of photo-generated charge carriers. The use of narrow bandgap semiconductor Cu2O modification to construct heterojunctions has also attracted widespread attention.4,5 In theory, the difference in band structure between TiO2 and Cu2O can easily lead to the formation of type Ⅱ heterojunctions,6 S-type heterojunctions,7 and Z-type heterojunctions.8 However, TiO2 and Cu2O may not form heterostructures during preparation, or the resulting heterostructures may not significantly improve catalytic activity.9 The catalytic performance of heterojunction materials is related to the morphology, interfacial contact, dispersibility, and oxygen vacancy defects.10,11,12,13 Among them, the heterojunction with strong interface contact is helpful to electron transfer, and the oxygen vacancies can also provide more active sites for CO2 adsorption. Xue et al.14 prepared a p-type Cu2O nanoparticle-coated n-type TiO2 nanotube (TNTs) array-based coaxial heterostructure using a combination of anodization and electrodeposition methods. It was found that the ribs formed during anodization and the added thiourea during electrodeposition played a crucial role in forming the Cu2O nanoparticle heterostructure. Bai et al.15 fabricated a uniform p-Cu2O/n-TiO2 heterojunction electrode using electrochemical anodization and pulse electrodeposition methods, which exhibited enhanced photoelectrocatalytic (PEC) activity for the degradation of chloramphenicol. Wei et al.16 stabilized Cu2O by adjusting the exposed surfaces and structural defects of TiO2, showing that oxygen vacancy defects enhanced charge separation and effective removal of oxidized holes of Cu2O. However, the fabrication methods for Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunctions are complex and not conducive to large-scale production. Although small-sized samples increase surface area, they are more prone to aggregation, thereby reducing catalytic performance.17 Meanwhile, excessive bulk oxygen vacancies can also create electron traps,18 which are detrimental to catalytic reactions. Therefore, controlling the ratio of surface oxygen vacancies to bulk oxygen vacancies is crucial for improving performance. This work uses a simple one-step hydrothermal method to prepare Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunction photocatalytic materials with strong interface contact, high dispersion, and oxygen vacancies. The experimental results indicate that an appropriate amount of Cu2+ is beneficial for improving photocatalytic properties, and the photocatalytic reaction mechanism of Cu2O/TiO2 with oxygen vacancies has been calculated using density functional theory (DFT). Results and discussion The influences of EDTA, sodium citrate, and copper acetate on the composition of samples are investigated. Generally, the XRD diffraction peak of Cu2O gradually increases with the increase of copper acetate. Comparing Figures 1A and S1A, it can be observed that as the amount of EDTA increases, the XRD diffraction peak of Cu2O decreases, while the diffraction peak of TiO2 remains unchanged. Comparing Figures 1A and S1B, it can be seen that as the amount of sodium citrate increases, the diffraction peak of Cu2O becomes more pronounced, while the diffraction peak of TiO2 is significantly affected. It indicates that EDTA and sodium citrate are essential in generating Cu2O and TiO2, respectively. fetched_contents.text: Interactions of Oxygen Vacancies with Photoinduced {Hole/Electron} Pairs in SrTiO3–x : Their Key Role in Photocatalytic H2 Production Abstract The present work elucidates the role of lattice oxygen vacancies (Vos) in SrTiO3 (STO) nanoparticles on the spin dynamics of photogenerated charge carriers (electrons/holes, e–/h+) and on the photocatalytic hydrogen (H2) evolution from H2O. Vo-enriched STO materials (Vo-STO) were synthesized via anoxic flame spray pyrolysis (A-FSP) technology that allowed production of a library of SrTiO3–x nanomaterials with controlled Vo concentrations. The optimal Vo-STO materials exhibited a 200% increase in photocatalytic H2 production rates compared with pristine STO. A combined study using electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy and photoelectrochemistry reveals that monomeric oxygen vacancies (type-B Vos) are the key factors to boost photoinduced charge separation via suppression of the e–/h+ recombination. Mott–Schottky and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy show that increased surface Vo population results in a slight upshift of flat band potential (E fb) and decreases the interfacial charge-transfer resistance, hence enhancing photocatalytic activity. Furthermore, open-circuit potential decay measurements reveal longer e–/h+ carrier lifetimes in Vo-rich SrTiO3–x . The present findings highlight the potential of Vo-spin engineering toward fine-tuning the electronic properties and photocatalytic activity of perovskite oxides. Technology wise, the present study exemplifies A-FSP as a versatile, industrial scale technology for the synthesis of Vo-enriched perovskite nanomaterials. ---------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------- 1. Since 1970, photocatalytic H2 production from H2O using solar irradiation has demonstrated great potential and has led to extensive research on semiconductor-based materials. , Among various photocatalysts, strontium titanate (SrTiO3) (STO) is established as a promising Ti perovskite due to its structural stability and favorable energy alignment for photocatalysis, i.e., its conduction band edge is ∼200 mV more negative than that of TiO2 which enhances the transfer of excited electrons to electron acceptors and possesses a moderate band gap (3.2 eV) photoactivated under UVA-irradiation. , So far, numerous efforts have focused on improving the spectral response of SrTiO3, e.g., including doping with metals , or nonmetals , as well as via heterojunction formation with other semiconductors. However, SrTiO3 faces the challenge of a rather high electron–hole (e–/h+) recombination rate which significantly hinders its photocatalytic activity, and therefore, the decrease of the (e–/h+) recombination rate is a key factor to improve the photocatalytic performance. In this context, oxygen vacancies (Vos) may play a key role in the photocatalytic efficiency of SrTiO3. In general Vos in oxide semiconductors constitute intrinsic lattice defects that may affect decisively the photocatalytic processes. − Particularly, in SrTiO3, oxygen vacancies have been shown to modulate its electronic structure; thus, if optimized, Vos can enhance its photocatalytic activity and photoelectrochemical (PEC) performance. Specifically, surface Vos can improve the photoinduced (e–/h+) separation, adsorption, and activation of H2O molecules on the surface, further boosting photocatalytic activity. , In contrast, bulk Vos appear to function primarily as deep (e–/h+) traps, leading to an increase in the recombination of photogenerated (e–/h+) pairs, which in turn diminishes photocatalytic activity. , Hence, controlled introduction of Vos on a photocatalyst, specifically through simultaneous control of their concentration and spatial distribution, surface versus bulk, is essential for systematically enhancing overall photocatalytic performance. , So far, Mao et al. used high-pressure/high-temperature hydrogenation to reduce TiO2, thus creating ‘black TiO2’, with a disordered Vo layer plus Ti3+ centers, leading to improved solar-driven photocatalytic H2 activity. In other pertinent studies, surface Vos were shown to promote photocatalytic performance, e.g., in TiO2, − ZnO, , WO3, and CeO2. fetched_contents.text: Role of oxygen vacancies on the structural, electronic, optical, and photocatalytic properties of Ba2CeMO6 (M = Bi, Sb) double perovskites: a DFT study Introduction Perovskite materials with the structure ABO3 have long been investigated in the last few decades due to their diverse applicability and unusual properties. Photo-catalysis1,2,3 is one of the greatest applications of these materials. With the concern of rapid industrialization and fast population growth in the twenty-first century, it is crucial to focus on sustainable energy production. However, due to extensive research and limited potential scope, the structure became obstacles to success. Double perovskite (A2B/B//O6) materials work on these limitations and provide versatility to design novel characteristics with the suitable combination of A and B site atoms. In particular, rare-earth-based double perovskite materials, in the current research history found to exhibit strong photocatalytic activities due to their unique crystal structure and novel charge separation mechanism. The presence of mixed valence states makes the compound superior in facilitating photo-active charge carriers as well as enhancing conductivity4,5,6. Among various compounds, Ce-based materials are found to be promising for suitable photocatalytic applications7 owing to the unique redox flexibility of cerium (Ce³⁺/Ce⁴⁺), which can strongly influence defect chemistry, electronic structure, and photocatalytic behavior. From the previous research on rare-earth-based double perovskite, it is observed that variation of synthesis technique led to the formation of polymorphic structures. For example, Hatakeyama et al. in 20108 prepared several rare-earth-based Ba2LnBiO6 (Ln = La, Ce, Nd, Sm, Eu, Gd, Dy) double perovskite using the solid-state method and found cubic structure of those compounds. Their concern is to substitution of Bi3+ in Ba2Bi3+Bi5+O6 frame. In contrast, several other research groups reported monoclinic structure of these compounds via the citrate pyrolysis technique. For instance, Arisa Sato et al. obtained9 monoclinic crystal structure of Ba2PrBiO6. Additionally, Roy et al. also reported monoclinic structure of Ba2TbBiO6 compound10. The compounds Ba2PrSbO69 and Ba2TbSbO610 were found to possess cubic structures when prepared by the citrate method; however, the same compounds exhibited monoclinic phases when synthesized via the solid-state route11. This clearly indicates polymorphism or phase relaxation behavior of rare-earth-based double perovskite materials. To explore this phenomenon, earlier studies have used the tolerance factor formula, a key tool for analyzing the stability of different phases. These studies identified charge-disproportionation-related mixed phases within the structure and consequently proposed modifications to the conventional tolerance factor model9,10. Although their approaches were valid for specific systems, they failed to explain phase stability in other compositions, like rare-earth-based double perovskite. Therefore, it is necessary to establish a more general formula with the involvement of key parameters that can clearly mitigate the problem. The present study focuses on this issue and aims to modify the conventional tolerance factor equation. Study reveals that oxygen deficiency is a major concern for the high-temperature synthesis of these oxide compounds12,13,14,15,16, which suddenly leads to the transformation of semiconducting to metallic structure17,18,19,20,21. For instance, Hatakeyama suggested defect in their crystal leads to the formation of Ba2LnBiO6(Ln = La, Ce, Nd, Sm, Eu, Gd, Dy) compounds. It is observed that a defect in the crystal, especially oxygen, can transform the crystallographic phase12,22,23,24,25,26,27. Recent advances in photocatalysis have demonstrated that rational control of electronic structure, defect chemistry, and interfacial charge transfer is crucial for achieving high photocatalytic efficiency. In particular, state-of-the-art studies reported in28,29 have highlighted the importance of defect engineering and electronic structure modulation in enhancing photocatalytic performance of complex oxide and semiconductor systems. These developments further emphasize the need for a fundamental theoretical understanding of structure–property relationships in emerging photocatalytic materials, such as Ce-based double perovskites. We consider oxygen defects due to lighter elements are mainly responsible for this polymorphism of Ba2CeMO6 (M = Bi, Sb) double perovskite, and try to correlate the experimental results through first-principles calculations. In this research, we focus on the Ba2CeMO6 (M = Bi, Sb) double perovskite, a newly synthesized compound30, which exhibits strong photocatalytic behavior. It is observed that the Ce-based compounds, such as CeO2 nanoparticles31, Cerium-doped TiO232, ZnO/CeO233, exhibit strong visible-light photocatalytic activity due to the Ce3+/Ce4+ redox couple and improved charge separation. We address this critical theoretical gap through comprehensive density functional theory calculations. Our study aims to uncover (i) the fundamental origin of heterophase coexistence in Ce-based double perovskites and (ii) the intrinsic electronic and defect-related factors governing their photocatalytic activity. By providing atomistic-level insights into the interplay between crystal structure, cation valence states, and oxygen defects, this work establishes a theoretical framework to support and guide future experimental design of Ce-based double perovskite photocatalysts. Besides, investigated its intriguing physical aspects accompanied by several artificial oxygen vacancies. The core mechanism linking oxygen vacancies to improved photocatalytic efficiency is that vacancies act as defect-mediated intermediaries between light absorption, charge generation, and surface reaction, altering both electronic structure and transport dynamics. The evidence points to a central role of vacancy-induced surface states or trap states that modify the band structure. A direct study states that oxygen vacancies create intermediate electronic states that reduce the band gap, which is a clear indication of band-structure modification [N1-R4]. Another source says oxygen vacancies suppress electron–hole recombination and lead to enhanced photocatalytic degradation, showing that vacancies influence the electronic landscape in a way that favors charge separation [N1-F1]. In addition, the DFT study on Ba2CeMO6 double perovskites explains that oxygen vacancies are used to correlate structural, electronic, optical, and photocatalytic properties and that vacancy-induced property changes are analyzed at the atomic level [N5-F4].

Oxygen vacancies influence charge carrier generation, separation, and recombination in three main ways. First, they can act as trapping sites for photogenerated electrons, promoting charge separation [N1-R1]. Second, vacancies can reduce recombination by suppressing electron–hole recombination, as shown in the BaSn1−xCuxO3 study [N1-F1]. Third, they can create fast charge transport channels, with one source indicating that oxygen vacancies modulate dynamics of photogenerated carriers at interfaces [N2-R2]. The charge-separation literature also notes that charge separation can occur via asymmetric energetics, asymmetric kinetics, or hybrid modes, and vacancies are therefore relevant as they can alter these energetic and kinetic conditions [N1-R5].

Vacancy density, position, and coordination affect catalytic activity in a non-uniform way. The evidence explicitly notes that oxygen vacancies can serve as active sites for charge storage or degradation of contaminants [N1-R3]. It also shows that oxygen vacancies created by substitution of Sn4+ by Cu2+ improve performance, implying that vacancy position and coordination are important [N1-F1]. The SrTiO3 study emphasizes that controlled introduction of oxygen vacancies, especially by controlling their concentration and spatial distribution, is essential for enhancing overall photocatalytic performance [N4-F3]. In other words, vacancies are not simply “more is better” but must be tuned to avoid excessive recombination and to optimize their role as either surface states, transport mediators, or reaction sites. The same study also notes that surface vacancies can improve photoinduced charge separation, whereas bulk vacancies can act as deep traps [N4-F3]. This distinction means that vacancy coordination and location—surface versus bulk—dramatically change whether a vacancy enhances or limits activity.

Overall, the core mechanism is vacancy-induced electronic restructuring plus defect-mediated charge dynamics. Vacancies modify the band structure through intermediate states or reduced band gaps [N1-R4], suppress recombination by trapping electrons [N1-R1], and promote charge separation via interface coupling and transport [N2-R2]. At the same time, vacancy density, position, and coordination determine whether the defect functions as an active site, a recombination center, or a transport channel [N1-R3][N4-F3].

Heterostructured oxide systems exploit oxygen vacancies primarily by using them as defect-mediated interfaces that improve charge transport and interfacial coupling. The evidence shows that heterojunction design and interface coupling can enhance charge transport, with one study specifically highlighting “fast charge transport channels at the interfaces modulated by oxygen vacancies” [N2-R2]. Another source connects heterostructure engineering with oxygen vacancy engineering as promising strategies to reinforce Zn²⁺ ion storage, even though the cited excerpt is broader, it supports the idea that vacancy engineering can be used to optimize heterostructure performance [N2-R4]. A heterostructured example is also provided in Cu2O/TiO2: the study reports that oxygen vacancies improve photocatalytic activity, and that appropriate interface contact, dispersibility, and oxygen vacancy defects are important for catalytic performance [N3-F2]. In this system, the heterojunction itself is designed to strengthen electron transfer, while oxygen vacancies provide additional active sites and influence charge separation [N3-F2].

Vacancies can act as recombination centers or mediators at interfaces. The SrTiO3 study explicitly distinguishes between surface and bulk oxygen vacancies: surface vacancies are key factors to boost photoinduced charge separation via suppression of e–/h+ recombination, whereas bulk vacancies appear to function primarily as deep traps that increase recombination [N4-F3]. This is important because heterostructures often involve interfacial regions where charge transfer is most sensitive to defect distribution. The same study also states that an optimal Vo-STO material exhibited a 200% increase in photocatalytic H2 production rates compared with pristine STO, showing that vacancy-mediated interface effects can dominate performance [N4-F3]. The heterostructured BaSn1−xCuxO3 example also shows that oxygen vacancies suppress electron–hole recombination and improve charge separation [N1-F1], which reinforces the idea that vacancies can mediate, rather than destroy, interfacial charge transport.

Heterostructure geometry changes vacancy-mediated electron/hole pathways by altering the spatial distribution and accessibility of vacancies. The Cu2O/TiO2 study reports that oxygen vacancies are created in heterojunctions and that their presence is linked to improved CO2 reduction performance [N3-F2]. The study also emphasizes that heterojunctions with strong interface contact are helpful for electron transfer, and that oxygen vacancies can provide more active sites for CO2 adsorption [N3-F2]. This means that geometry—not just the presence of vacancies—controls how vacancies are positioned relative to charge carriers and reaction sites. The SrTiO3 study similarly notes that controlling vacancy concentration and spatial distribution is essential for systematic enhancement of performance [N4-F3]. Together, these examples show that heterostructures can be designed to make vacancies more effective as transport mediators or recombination suppressors, depending on whether the geometry favors surface or bulk vacancy access [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In summary, heterostructured oxide systems use oxygen vacancies by combining interface coupling and heterojunction design to improve charge transport [N2-R2][N2-R4], while vacancies can act as either recombination centers or mediators depending on their location and coordination [N4-F3]. Geometry determines the pathways through which vacancies influence electrons and holes, making vacancy-mediated charge transport a tunable rather than fixed effect [N3-F2].

The experimental and computational evidence supporting the role of oxygen vacancies is substantial and spans multiple complementary techniques and performance metrics. On the experimental side, oxygen vacancies are detected and their local environment probed by several techniques. One study uses XPS and EPR results to show the presence of oxygen vacancies [N4-R5]. Another source explicitly states that EPR is used to investigate the role of oxygen vacancies and that EPR signals can indicate oxygen vacancies [N6-R3]. In situ EPR technology is also used in the photo-switchable oxygen vacancy study to investigate the dynamic evolution of oxygen vacancies during photocatalytic reactions [N6-R1]. These methods are important because they distinguish between static vacancy formation and dynamic vacancy behavior, and they can probe both surface and bulk vacancies [N6-R3][N6-R1].

XPS and EPR are particularly useful for detecting vacancy density and local environment. The Cu2O/TiO2 study reports high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and EPR studies showing optimal oxygen vacancy in the most effective heterojunction [N3-F2]. The same study also uses XPS testing and fitting of XPS spectra to identify Cu2p orbitals and Cu+ states, which indirectly supports the presence of oxygen vacancies by showing a changed surface chemistry [N3-F2]. The SrTiO3 study similarly uses EPR and photoelectrochemistry to show that monomeric oxygen vacancies are key to boosting charge separation and that vacancy population changes the electronic behavior [N4-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a direct experimental pipeline: XPS identifies surface composition changes, EPR identifies unpaired electrons and vacancy-like states, and in situ EPR captures vacancy dynamics [N4-R5][N6-R3][N6-R1].

Performance metrics demonstrating improved photocatalytic activity include photocatalytic rate constants, degradation percentages, and yield. The BaSn1−xCuxO3 study reports that Cu-doped BaSnO3 exhibits an 8-times higher rate constant than the parent phase under visible light and a 60-times higher rate constant under sunlight [N1-F1]. It also states that degradation percentages of MB are more than 95% in the doped phase in 30 minutes, compared with much slower degradation in the parent phase [N1-F1]. The Cu2O/TiO2 study reports a CO yield of 10.22 μmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹, which is 1.85 times that of TiO2, with the best performance occurring at an optimal Cu mass fraction [N3-F2]. These metrics are direct demonstrations that oxygen vacancies can translate into improved activity, even when vacancy concentration and coordination are tuned [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Theoretical results explain vacancy-induced property changes by showing how vacancies alter electronic structure, optical properties, and charge transport. The DFT study on Ba2CeMO6 double perovskites uses first-principles calculations to correlate oxygen vacancies with structural, electronic, optical, and photocatalytic properties, and it explicitly states that vacancy-induced property changes are analyzed at the atomic level [N5-F4]. Another DFT study on oxygen vacancies in oxides determines EOvac and finds that band gap modulation is a major consequence [N5-R4]. The review on oxygen vacancies in Cu2O/TiO2 notes that DFT calculations indicate a lower energy barrier for CO2-to-CO conversion in the oxygen-vacancy system, showing how vacancies can stabilize reaction pathways [N3-F2]. Together, these theoretical results provide a mechanistic basis for the experimental observations: vacancies modify electronic states, change optical behavior, and lower reaction barriers [N5-F4][N5-R4][N3-F2].

Overall, the evidence is strong and multidisciplinary. Experimental detection is provided by XPS, EPR, and in situ EPR [N4-R5][N6-R3][N6-R1], performance is shown by rate constants, degradation, and yield [N1-F1][N3-F2], and theory explains vacancy-induced band gap modulation and electronic restructuring [N5-F4][N5-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that oxygen vacancies are not just incidental defects but deliberately engineered features whose role is best understood through integrated experimental and computational analysis.

Oxygen vacancies mediate surface reactions by serving as active sites for adsorption, activation, and reaction intermediates. The evidence states that oxygen vacancies leave behind two unpaired electrons and serve as adsorption and reaction sites on metal oxide surfaces [N6-R5]. It also reports that oxygen vacancies are the major structural defects on TiO2(110) and that they are important for surface chemistry [N6-R2]. The SrTiO3 study similarly notes that surface vacancies can improve adsorption and activation of H2O molecules on the surface, which boosts photocatalytic activity [N4-F3]. In the Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunction, oxygen vacancies are linked to more active sites for CO2 adsorption and improved charge separation [N3-F2]. In the Cu2O/TiO2 heterojunction, oxygen vacancies are linked to more active sites for CO2 adsorption and improved charge separation [N3-F2]. These sources together show that vacancies are not passive defects but active participants in surface chemistry, providing sites where reactants can adsorb, activate, and proceed through reaction pathways [N6-R5][N4-F3][N3-F2].

Vacancy density and dynamics change during light irradiation or reaction. The photo-switchable oxygen vacancy study uses in situ EPR technology to investigate the dynamic evolution of oxygen vacancies during photocatalytic reactions, showing that vacancies are not static but can change during irradiation [N6-R1]. The same study notes that oxygen vacancies are “dynamic active sites” and that their behavior is monitored in situ [N6-R1]. The SrTiO3 study also reports that oxygen vacancies can be created by calcination under H2 and that a Vo-rich surface can be produced by reduction, demonstrating that vacancy formation and evolution are process-dependent [N4-F3]. The CuO study further shows that oxygen vacancies can be dynamically engineered in real time through simple alkali etching without interrupting the reaction, which is a direct demonstration of vacancy dynamics during catalytic operation [N6-R4]. These examples indicate that vacancy density is not fixed but responds to light, heat, or chemical treatment during catalysis [N6-R1][N4-F3][N6-R4].

Surface reaction dynamics affect overall photocatalytic performance because they control the availability of active sites and the efficiency of charge-carrier utilization. The SrTiO3 study shows that surface vacancies improve photoinduced charge separation and that controlling their concentration and spatial distribution is essential for performance [N4-F3]. The Cu2O/TiO2 study reports that oxygen vacancies improve photocatalytic activity and that the best performance is obtained when vacancy concentration and interface quality are optimized [N3-F2]. The same study also notes that excessive bulk vacancies can create electron traps, which are detrimental to catalytic reactions [N3-F2]. In other words, vacancy dynamics influence not only whether a reaction can occur but also whether it proceeds efficiently and selectively. The dynamic nature of vacancies means that performance is not only determined by their initial concentration but also by their real-time behavior during irradiation and reaction [N6-R1][N4-F3][N3-F2].

### 5) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports support a single integrated picture: oxygen vacancies improve photocatalytic efficiency and charge transfer in heterostructured oxide systems by acting as defect-mediated electronic and transport intermediaries. They modify the band structure through intermediate states or reduced band gaps [N1-R4], suppress recombination by trapping electrons [N1-R1], and promote charge separation via interface coupling and transport [N2-R2]. At the same time, vacancies serve as active sites for adsorption, activation, and reaction intermediates [N6-R5], and their density, position, and coordination determine whether they enhance or limit performance [N1-R3][N4-F3]. Heterostructured systems can be engineered to exploit vacancies by using them as defect-mediated interfaces, thereby improving charge transport while controlling recombination [N2-R2][N3-F2]. Experimental detection is provided by XPS, EPR, and in situ EPR [N4-R5][N6-R3][N6-R1], performance is shown by rate constants, degradation, and yield [N1-F1][N3-F2], and theory explains vacancy-induced band gap modulation and electronic restructuring [N5-F4][N5-R4]. Overall, the evidence shows that oxygen vacancies are not incidental defects but deliberately engineered features whose role is best understood through integrated experimental and computational analysis [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4].
